findings.claim: orders 10-01 has 164 data rows (9,026 bytes). Orders 09-30 has 461 rows (25,028 bytes). That is about 36% of the prior day. Both files have the contract header, no missing or extra columns, no parse problems and a trailing newline. The last line is complete, so there is no cut-off line or malformed row.

The ordered_at hours (order_ts in the file) for 10-01 cover only hours 00–08, with 12–24 orders per hour and nothing from 09:00 onward. 09-30 has all 24 hours with 12–29 per hour. Per-hour volume is normal for the hours present, so the data stops early in the day. The hourly counts come from raw.orders, whose 10-01 total of 164 matches the landing file.

The 10-01 file is not filtered. All three channels (app, marketplace, web) and all four statuses (placed, shipped, cancelled, returned) are present, with currency USD only. The same is true on 09-30. The channel mix on 10-01 is app 51, marketplace 39, web 74. On 09-30 it is app 139, marketplace 80, web 242. The shares are roughly similar, so no single channel, status or currency is missing.

order_items 10-01 has 334 rows and payments 10-01 has 157 rows. Both have valid headers, no parse problems and complete last lines. Order_items ends at order 13841 and payments ends at order 13839. The payments timestamps I saw are all early-morning (01:30–04:54), which fits the same early cutoff. I did not check the full payments distribution, payment methods or the 09-30 order_items and payments files. I only saw card and gift_card in the first lines.

customers 10-01 has 30 rows (ids 2871–2900), all with signup_date 2026-10-01, country US in the lines shown, and a clean header. It does not show the same obvious truncation. I did not compare it with 09-30.

The landing inspection returned no manifest, trailer or expected-row-count info for any file, so a manifest mismatch can't be confirmed or ruled out. The ingest_config is empty for these tables, so no ingest setting is dropping rows.

evidence.text:
## Symptoms
- dbt tests fail: `unique_stg_orders_order_id`, `unique_stg_order_items_order_item_id`, `unique_stg_payments_payment_id` or similar, with N failing rows.
- `reconciliation:raw.orders->marts.fct_orders` fails: mart row count exceeds distinct raw orders.
- Revenue for a day is inflated; `row_count_trend` may fail on the high side (above 160%).
- Staging models do no dedup, so duplicates in raw flow straight to marts.

## Symptoms
- `ingest` fails: `landing file missing: landing/<table>/dt=<date>/<table>.csv` (loud).
- Check `partition_present:raw.<table>` fails: `raw.<table> partition <date> has 0 rows` (silent: an empty file loads fine).
- Check `row_count_trend:raw.<table>` fails: today's rows fall outside 60%-160% of the trailing 7-partition median.
- Check `reconciliation:raw.orders->marts.fct_orders` fails: distinct raw orders for the day differ from `fct_orders` rows.
- Check `freshness:marts.fct_orders` fails: latest order date in the mart is behind the partition.
- Business symptom: revenue or order count for a day looks too low.

## Verification
- Rerun the partition. `partition_present`, `row_count_trend` and `reconciliation` must pass.
- Row counts for the day are now within the normal range of prior days.
- Hour and channel distributions match prior days.
- `assert_order_totals_match_items` and `assert_payments_match_orders` pass.

## The evidence-citation habit
- Every claim in a ticket or handoff carries an id. Examples:
  - `run 3f2a9c1e, step ingest, log:412`
  - `ops.dq_results check_id=row_count_trend:raw.orders observed=45%`
  - `raw.orders _dt=<date> _source_file=landing/orders/dt=<date>/orders.csv`
- A reader should be able to re-run your queries and see the same thing.
- State what you ruled out, not just what you found.

args.query: partial export filtered export low traffic owner escalation

evidence.text:
## Step 1: Which tables are affected?
- Compare row counts by `_dt` for `orders`, `order_items`, `payments` against the previous 7 days.
- Orders, items and payments are related. A drop in one with others normal suggests a partial export of that table.
- If all three dropped by a similar proportion, the export for the day was truncated or filtered across tables.

## Step 3: Partial vs filtered
- Partial (truncated) export: the file ends early. Rows are cut off by time: early hours present and late hours missing.
- Filtered export: a whole slice is absent regardless of time: e.g. one `channel` or one `status` has no rows, while the rest of the distribution looks normal.
- Compare today's distribution with prior days:
  - orders by hour of `order_ts`
  - orders by `channel`
  - orders by `status`
  - payments by `method`
- A chart or table of share-by-hour and share-by-channel for today vs a typical day makes the gap obvious.
- Record which hours or which category are missing; this is your evidence for the upstream ticket.

## Escalation
- Model logic or intentional change: `analytics_engineering`.
- Export or file problem persisting after redelivery: `upstream_app_team`.
- Infrastructure or orchestration: `data_platform`.

## Remedy for one-off export glitches
- Use `request_upstream_redelivery` for the day with ALL affected related tables together: `orders`, `order_items`, and `payments` (add `customers` only if it is also affected).
- Redelivery re-runs the export and produces a correct file for each table.
- Redelivering just `orders` when items/payments were also cut leaves referential mismatches.
- Then rerun the partition and verify.

structured.answer: The runbooks treat a row_count_trend failure as a missing, partial or filtered data problem. They separate partial from filtered exports by the shape of the gap, and they recommend upstream redelivery of all related tables together. I found no section on how to recognise a genuine low-traffic day, and no owner named specifically for row_count_trend. The nearest owner guidance is `upstream_app_team` for export problems that persist after redelivery.

findings.claim: row_count_trend:raw.<table> fails when the day's rows fall outside 60%-160% of the trailing 7-partition median. A low result points to missing, partial or filtered data. A high result (above 160%) can instead indicate duplicates.

Step 1 is to compare row counts by _dt for orders, order_items and payments against the previous 7 days. If only one table dropped, that suggests a partial export of that table. If all three dropped by a similar proportion, the export was truncated or filtered across tables.

Partial (truncated) export: the file ends early, so early hours are present and late hours are missing. Filtered export: a whole slice is absent regardless of time, such as one channel or status with no rows, while the rest of the distribution looks normal. To tell them apart, compare today's distribution with prior days by order_ts hour, channel, status and payment method. Record which hours or categories are missing, because that is the evidence for the upstream ticket.

Remedy for one-off export glitches: use request_upstream_redelivery for the day with ALL affected related tables together (orders, order_items and payments, plus customers only if it is also affected). Redelivering only orders when items and payments were also cut leaves referential mismatches. Then rerun the partition.

Verification: after the rerun, partition_present, row_count_trend and reconciliation must pass. Row counts must be back in the normal range, and the hour and channel distributions must match prior days. assert_order_totals_match_items and assert_payments_match_orders must also pass.

Owner: an export or file problem that persists after redelivery goes to `upstream_app_team`. Model or intentional logic changes go to `analytics_engineering`. Infrastructure or orchestration problems go to `data_platform`. This comes from the failed_jobs escalation section, not a section written for row_count_trend. The upstream ticket should carry the evidence from the partial-vs-filtered step.

The runbooks cite ops.dq_results rows (for example check_id=row_count_trend:raw.orders observed=45%) as the form of evidence to use in tickets. The only implied way to rule out a genuine low-traffic day is that hour and channel distributions look normal and the drop is not mirrored across related tables. That is my inference, not an explicit runbook rule.

I've proposed an upstream redelivery of orders, order_items and payments for 2026-10-01, followed by a rerun.

root_cause.explanation: Upstream delivered truncated 2026-10-01 exports for orders (164 vs median 461), order_items (334 vs 933) and payments (157 vs 439). Orders cover only hours 00-08, and per-hour volume is normal for those hours. All channels and statuses are present, so this is a partial export, not a filtered one. The files are structurally clean, no dbt model changed and the ingest config is the default, so the pipeline did not drop the rows. Customers is at its normal 30 rows.

evidence.claim: The run failed at quality_checks on the row_count_trend checks for raw.orders, raw.order_items and raw.payments, each at 36% of its trailing median.

Orders on 10-01 stop at 08:59, while 09-30 covers all 24 hours. All channels, statuses and USD are present, which points to a truncated export, not a filtered one.
No model changes and an empty ingest config rule out a pipeline-side cause.
Customers is unaffected, at 30 rows as in every partition.
For a one-off partial export, the runbook says to redeliver all affected related tables together and then rerun.
